claims.text: PGM-based nanoscale catalysts can catalyze ethanol oxidation with high activity.
The catalytic performance in ethanol oxidation is governed by a dynamic equilibrium between metallic and oxidized surface states.
Increasing electrode potential reversibly forms transient surface oxide species such as PtOx.
Transient surface oxides alter the adsorption energies of ethanol and its intermediates.
Oxide-induced adsorption-energy changes enhance ethanol-oxidation activity and selectivity.
Reversible surface oxidation preserves catalyst durability.
The baseline catalyst surface is predominantly metallic and has minimal oxide coverage.
Increasing electrode potential increases the formation of transient PGM-oxide species.
The relevant structural mediator is the reversible formation and removal of PtO, PtO2, or related PGM oxides.
Surface oxidation enhances the kinetics of proton-coupled electron-transfer steps in ethanol oxidation.
Complete ethanol oxidation involves transfer of 12 electrons and 12 protons.
Increasing potential will nonlinearly enhance ethanol-oxidation current density up to an optimal potential window.
Increasing potential within the optimal window will shift selectivity toward more complete oxidation products such as CO2.
Excessive oxide formation beyond the optimal potential window may reduce catalytic performance.
The proposed mechanism applies under electrochemical conditions where surface oxidation is reversible.
The proposed mechanism may fail at extreme potentials that cause irreversible oxidation.
The proposed mechanism may not apply in non-electrochemical reaction environments.
